sub_themes.sub_theme: duty cycle design for reef hydrophones

insights.claim: Denser sampling around dawn and dusk can extend deployments to a year without losing chorus structure.
Subsampling a multi-year, multi-site archive can test candidate duty cycles before committing to them.
Snapping shrimp energy up to 20 kHz justifies keeping 48 kHz sampling despite storage costs.
Sensitivity drift could be modelled against fouling scores from recovery photos and deployment duration.
The shrimp noise floor is a tempting internal calibration reference but varies seasonally.
Calibration tones at deployment and recovery can anchor drift correction when retrieval is infrequent.

sub_themes.sub_theme: validation of acoustic indices for reef biodiversity

insights.claim: Acoustic indices like ACI were adopted because they are easy, not because they were validated against fish abundance.
ACI may track shrimp activity or boat noise rather than fish, sometimes moving opposite to fish counts.
A single acoustic index probably cannot stand in for reef recovery after bleaching.
Occurrence of specific fish choruses is a more meaningful recovery measure than broadband indices, despite being harder.
Weak, sign-flipping index-abundance correlations warrant reporting when and why indices fail, tested across independent regions.
A well-documented multi-year, multi-reef recording archive may be more valuable than any single analysis.
Releasing ready-made features alongside raw audio makes the archive usable for ML researchers and oceanographers.
Publishing deployment logs, fouling scores and calibration notes prevents reusers being misled by sensitivity drift.
Embeddings pretrained on bird or urban audio may not transfer to reef audio with its shrimp noise floor.
Self-supervised learning could exploit tens of thousands of unlabelled reef hours if engineering capacity exists.
A large reef archive with an expert-labelled test set could serve as a hard benchmark for audio ML researchers.
Flagging and clustering unattributed calls matters ecologically because unknown sounds may be the most interesting.
Episodic few-shot training and pipeline building need a machine learning collaborator alongside the ecological expertise.

adjacent_ideas.claim: Correcting fouling-driven sensitivity drift might explain part of the sign flips between acoustic indices and fish counts.
Call rates from a few-shot call detector could become the event-based ground truth against which indices are validated.
Sparser duty cycles may bias detector-based chorus occurrence metrics more than broadband index values.
An open archive could include an open-set task where models must surface unattributed recurring reef calls.
